title: The repository pattern (and when it's overkill); testing DB code on real Postgres
summary: A repository is a concrete type that owns its SQL and speaks domain values and errors; an interface appears only where a consumer needs a substitute. The rules that matter live in the database, so test repositories on a real PostgreSQL, one rolled-back transaction per test.

examples.title: The same service over a fake and over PostgreSQL

annotations.note: The consumer declares the interface, with only the method it calls. The repository doesn't name it and doesn't need to: Go interfaces are satisfied implicitly.

The repository owns the SQL and translates driver errors at the boundary: callers see ErrEmailTaken, never SQLSTATE 23505 or a *pgconn.PgError. It is a concrete struct; nothing here needs an interface of its own.
A fake encodes what you believe the database does: here, exact-match uniqueness. It is fast and fine for testing signup's own logic, but it can't tell you whether the belief is true.
The real rule: a unique index on the expression lower(email). This is behaviour of your system that lives only in the schema, along with CHECK constraints, NULL semantics, collations and triggers.

Same service, two stores, two answers. A test suite built on the fake stays green while production returns "email already registered", which is why the repository itself must be tested against PostgreSQL.

examples.title: A table-driven test on real PostgreSQL, one rolled-back transaction per case

annotations.note: The repository asks for the one method it uses. *pgxpool.Pool, *pgx.Conn and pgx.Tx all have it, which is what lets a test hand it a transaction instead of the pool.

Connect and migrate once per test binary. Without DATABASE_URL the tests skip instead of failing, so go test ./... still works on a machine without a database. TestMain may return; the wrapper exits with m.Run's result.

Every test runs inside its own transaction, and Cleanup rolls it back: no test sees another's rows and nothing needs deleting. t.Context() (Go 1.24) is canceled just before cleanups run, so the rollback gets context.Background().
Table-driven: each case names the situation and the error it expects. The second case is the one the fake in the first example got wrong; the unique index answers it.
After the expected 23505 the transaction is aborted (lesson 3). That is fine because the case ends here; a test that keeps going after an expected error needs a savepoint.

use_cases: A concrete repository (or sqlc's Queries) called directly: CRUD services with one database and little logic, which is most of them
A consumer-declared interface plus a fake: business logic with real branching that should be unit-tested in microseconds
Interfaces with two real implementations, like this app's httpapi.Runner (in-process runner and Docker runner client)
Integration tests on real PostgreSQL: every repository, every query with constraints, NULLs or collations involved
strengths: Unlike Java's interface-per-repository habit, Go's implicit interfaces let the consumer define the seam later, without touching the repository
Transactional DDL and cheap transactions make rolled-back tests fast enough to run on every change against a local PostgreSQL
Error translation in the repository keeps driver types out of services and handlers, so storage can change behind a stable API
Tests against the real database pin down behaviour no fake reproduces: expression indexes, constraint names, collations, NULL comparisons
weaknesses: Integration tests need a running PostgreSQL and a migrated schema; CI must provide one
A transaction per test can't cover code that must commit or that needs two sessions (lock waits, LISTEN/NOTIFY); those need a schema per test or cleanup
Interfaces added too early hide which implementation runs and multiply files for no gain

pitfalls.title: Mocking the driver
pitfalls.detail: A mocked pgx asserts the SQL text you expected to send, not what PostgreSQL does with it, so it passes while a constraint, a typo in a column or a NULL breaks production. Test repositories against PostgreSQL.

pitfalls.title: An interface per struct, by reflex
pitfalls.detail: A UserRepository interface beside its only implementation, declared by the producer, mirrors every method and protects nothing. Let each consumer declare the few methods it needs, when it needs a substitute.

pitfalls.title: Rolling back with t.Context() in Cleanup
pitfalls.detail: t.Context() is already canceled when cleanup functions run, so the ROLLBACK can't be sent and pgx closes the connection instead. Use context.Background() there.

pitfalls.title: Parallel tests that insert the same unique value
pitfalls.detail: Uncommitted rows are invisible to other transactions, but a unique index still makes the second insert wait until the first transaction ends. Give parallel tests distinct values.

pitfalls.title: Tests that depend on committed data
pitfalls.detail: Seeding shared rows that every test reads couples the tests to their order. Create what a test needs inside its own transaction.

quiz.q: Your fake user store passes every test, but production rejects "Ayse@Example.com" after "ayse@example.com". Why?
options: The fake has a bug in its map
The unique index on lower(email) is a database rule the fake never knew
quiz.why: A fake encodes your assumptions; the schema holds the actual rule, and only a test on PostgreSQL checks it.

quiz.q: A service has one storage implementation (sqlc over PostgreSQL) and almost no logic. Does it need a UserRepository interface?
options: Yes, always program to an interface
No: call the concrete store or Queries; add a small interface when a consumer needs a substitute
quiz.why: An interface earns its place with a second implementation or logic worth testing in isolation; otherwise it is indirection.

quiz.q: Which context should the rollback in t.Cleanup use?
quiz.why: t.Context() is canceled just before cleanups run, so a rollback using it can't reach the server.

quiz.q: Code under test calls WithTx(ctx, db, fn), and the test passes its own pgx.Tx as db. What happens?
options: It fails: you can't begin inside a transaction
Begin on a Tx creates a savepoint; the code's commit releases it, and the test's rollback still undoes everything
The inner commit makes the data permanent
quiz.why: pgx.Tx.Begin starts a pseudo nested transaction backed by a savepoint, so the outer rollback wins.

further_reading.title: package testing: TestMain, T.Cleanup, T.Context, T.Skip
package pgx: Tx and pseudo nested transactions

body:
## Concept

A **repository** is the type that owns the SQL for one part of the domain. It takes
domain values in, returns domain values and domain errors out (`User`, `ErrEmailTaken`),
and nothing above it imports pgx. In Go it is a plain struct with a constructor, often a
thin layer over sqlc's `Queries`.

Whether it also needs an **interface** is a separate question, answered by its consumers.
Add one when a consumer needs a substitute: business logic you want to unit-test with a
fake, or a second real implementation. The consumer declares it, with only the methods it
calls, and the repository satisfies it without knowing. Without such a consumer, an
interface is ceremony: one implementation, a mirror of its methods, and one more hop when
reading the code. That is when the pattern is overkill, and with sqlc's typed methods it
often is.

**Testing.** A repository's behaviour is half Go and half schema: unique indexes,
constraints, NULL handling, collations. Only a real PostgreSQL tests the second half, so
test repositories against one. The standard shape: connect and migrate once, give each
test a transaction, roll it back in `t.Cleanup`, and skip when no database is configured.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java: Spring Data generates an implementation behind `interface UserRepository`; in Go
  you write the struct, and interfaces come from consumers. Testcontainers plus a
  `@Transactional` test (rolled back by default in Spring tests) is the same
  real-database, rolled-back-transaction technique.
- Python: Django's `TestCase` wraps each test in a transaction and rolls it back; pytest
  fixtures with teardown play `t.Cleanup`'s role.
- JS/TS: mocking the database client in Jest tests the mock. The real-database approach
  is the same as here: a test database and a transaction or truncate per test.
- C: swapping in a fake object file at link time is the C version of a fake, with the
  same blind spot.

## Design notes

This app shows both sides. `httpapi.Runner` is an interface declared by its consumer,
the HTTP layer, because two real implementations exist: `runexec.Executor` runs lessons
in-process, `runclient.Client` forwards them to the Docker runner. The stores
(`*learningstore.Store`, `*runstore.Store`) are concrete and used directly, because there
is one database and nothing to swap.

Its database tests follow the integration pattern: `sqlrun_test.go` and
`multisession_test.go` in `server/internal/sqlrun` carry `//go:build integration` and read
`TEST_DATABASE_URL`, skipping when it is unset, while the unit tests in `split_test.go`
beside them have no tag. `go test ./...` stays fast, and `go test -tags integration ./...` runs the honest
suite against the local playground database. This lesson's runtime passes
`DATABASE_URL` instead and has no tags, which is why the example skips on the variable
alone.

A transaction per test covers code that accepts a `DBTX`-style interface. Code that
commits on its own can still run inside it if it begins from something you pass in:
`Begin` on a `pgx.Tx` makes a savepoint. Code that needs two sessions, waits on locks or
uses LISTEN needs committed data instead: a schema per test (what this runner does for
every run) or truncating tables between tests.

Case-insensitive rules carry a locale: `lower()` in this C.UTF-8 database maps `I` to
`i`, so a unique index on `lower(username)` treats `IŞIL` and `ışıl` as different users,
while `lower(username COLLATE "tr-x-icu")` would not. Behaviour like that is exactly what
a test on the real database pins down.

expected.fake-vs-real:
fake:
  ayse@example.com id=1 err=<nil>
  Ayse@Example.com id=2 err=<nil>
postgres:
  ayse@example.com id=1 err=<nil>
  Ayse@Example.com id=0 err=email already registered
